prompt:
You read a Twitter/X thread by Marius Hobbhahn (unrolled). Extract research choices and the reasoning he gives, as well as any views on how to do research.

Return 3-15 items. Each item is one of:
- "decision": a research decision he (or his team) made, where another choice was possible;
- "rejected": an option, method or line of work he rejected or argued against;
- "disagreement": a place where he disagrees with a default view or practice in the field;
- "advice": advice he gives about how to do research (what to work on, how to test, how to interpret results).
Prefer research methodology (evaluation design, experimental controls, what evidence to trust, which questions to pursue, how strongly to state claims) over biography, logistics or summaries of results. Only include items the text itself supports; return {"decisions": []} if there are none. For each item give:
- item_type: decision / rejected / disagreement / advice
- point: one of D1-D6 (D1 which experiment or hypothesis to pursue; D2 what evidence to collect; D3 whether to accept a result; D4 whether to continue or drop a line of work; D5 how to interpret an ambiguous result; D6 how strongly to state a claim)
- problem: the research problem or question faced, stated neutrally (1 sentence)
- did: what he chose, did or recommends (1 sentence)
- alternatives_named: a JSON list of strings, the alternatives the text itself names or rejects ([] if none)
- stated_reason: the reason the text gives ("" if none)
- quote: a VERBATIM passage of HIS OWN words, 15-60 words, copied character for character, that shows the item. Do not paraphrase, fix spelling or punctuation, merge passages, or use ellipses.
- off_topic: true if the item is not about AI, ML or research practice (e.g. energy policy, health, productivity), else false

Return only JSON: {"decisions": [{"item_type": ..., "point": ..., "problem": ..., "did": ..., "alternatives_named": [...], "stated_reason": ..., "quote": ..., "off_topic": ...}]}

 LLMs Often Know When They Are Being Evaluated!

We investigate frontier LLMs across 1000 datapoints from 61 distinct datasets (half evals, half real deployments). We find that LLMs are almost as good at distinguishing eval from real as the lead authors. 

 Paper: 

We take 1000 different transcripts, equally split between evals and real deployments and equally split between QA and agentic settings. We then ask the model to classify this as an eval or real deployment, aggregating five different questions arxiv.org/abs/2505.23836

 We find that models are often able to reason through the purpose of the transcript even in highly specific scenarios.

For example, they accurately identify that this prompt is a test for overrefusal using the word “stabbing”. 

 Quantitatively, we find that the models are almost as good as the lead authors at distinguishing eval from real deployment. 

The authors are very familiar with these benchmarks and have memory, so they should have a massive advantage. I’d treat this as an upper bound. I expect most humans would be way worse.

 Because we ask the AI to classify whether it’s an eval, we make it salient. In the real world, this might not be the case. 

Thus, we test a few other modes as well, e.g. testing the purpose of the transcript in different ways, including open-ended. 

 LLMs are able to identify the purpose of the transcript significantly better than random chance and especially Sonnet-3.7 is doing very well on the open-ended case. 

 We also investigated the reasons the model states for categorizing something as an eval vs. real deployment both qualitatively and quantitatively. 

 This project was done by my MATS scholars @jjpneedham and @gdedkins. We’re now starting our next project on how we can leverage these insights to build more realistic evals.

See matsprogram.org for details.
